note: Use of English round 3: 6 comprehension passages, 6 cloze passages, sentence interpretation, synonyms/antonyms in sentences, grammar, oral forms.

passages.title: The borehole at Umuahia Road
passages.text:
When the borehole at the end of Umuahia Road finally broke down, nobody was surprised. For eleven years it had served four hundred households, coughing up water at dawn and dusk while the council's own scheme lay rusting behind a locked gate. What surprised people was what happened next. Within a week, a committee of women had collected two hundred naira from every compound, hired a technician from Aba and replaced the pump. The council chairman, arriving with a camera crew to commission the 'repaired' borehole, was politely told that his help was no longer required.

The episode illustrates a pattern that development workers have observed across the country: communities are quickest to maintain what they have paid for themselves. Projects handed down from above, however generous, are treated as somebody else's property. When they fail, people wait for the giver to return. When a community's own money is at stake, the response is immediate.

This does not mean that government should abandon its responsibilities. It means, rather, that the manner of giving matters as much as the gift. A borehole that a community has helped to plan, fund and manage is far more likely to be pumping water in ten years' time than one that simply appeared one morning, complete with a plaque bearing a politician's name.

passages.title: Mr Bassey's mathematics class
passages.text:
Mr Bassey never announced a test. He simply walked in, wrote a single problem on the board and sat down to read his newspaper. The first time this happened, the class panicked; by the third week, it had become a ritual. Students learnt to arrive early, to check their previous night's work, and — most unusually — to explain their reasoning to one another in the minutes before he arrived, because whoever was called to the board would have to defend every line.

His methods were not universally admired. Parents complained that he set no homework in the conventional sense; the vice-principal noted that his lesson notes were never up to date. Yet when the results came, his classes outperformed every other in the zone, and had done so for nine consecutive years.

Asked once to explain his approach, he shrugged. 'I don't teach them mathematics,' he said. 'I make them uncomfortable enough to teach themselves.' Behind the modesty lay a firm conviction: that understanding is not something a teacher can transfer like a parcel, but something a learner must build, often painfully, by getting things wrong in front of others and discovering why.

passages.title: The market for second-hand clothes
passages.text:
Every Thursday, bales of used clothing arrive at the Katangowa market from ports in Lagos and Cotonou. Traders call them okrika, after the Rivers State town through which the first shipments reportedly passed decades ago. A single bale, bought unopened for a fixed price, may contain a fortune or a loss: the trader does not know until the ties are cut whether the contents are designer jackets or shapeless rags.

Critics argue that the trade has destroyed Nigeria's textile industry. In the 1980s the mills of Kaduna and Kano employed hundreds of thousands; today most stand silent. Cheap imported clothing, they say, made local cloth uncompetitive. Defenders of the trade reply that the mills were already failing from power shortages and smuggling, and that okrika now feeds more families than the mills ever did — the porters, sorters, menders, launderers and hawkers who form a chain from the bale to the buyer.

Both sides may be right. What is beyond dispute is that a poor family can clothe its children decently for a fraction of the cost of new garments, and that a government which bans the trade without providing an alternative will punish the poorest twice: once as workers and again as consumers.

passages.title: Grandmother and the mobile phone
passages.text:
My grandmother refused to own a mobile phone until she was seventy-six. Telephones, she maintained, were for people who had something urgent to say and nobody nearby to say it to. She had neither problem. Her compound was never empty; her news travelled by the older networks of church, market and the women who came to plait her hair.

What changed her mind was not persuasion but a funeral. Her sister died in Kaduna on a Tuesday; the letter announcing it reached her the following Monday, two days after the burial. She wept, not only for her sister but for the six days during which she had gone about her business, laughing and bargaining, while her sister lay in a mortuary eight hundred kilometres away.

The phone my uncle bought her was the simplest available. She learnt to answer it within a week and to make calls within a month. She never sent a text message in her life. But she kept the phone under her pillow at night, charged and switched on, and when it rang after dark she would answer it before the second ring, with the voice of a woman who had once been late for a death.

passages.title: Why the plastics ban stalled
passages.text:
In January the state government announced, with considerable fanfare, that single-use plastic bags would be banned within six months. Environmental groups applauded. Market women shrugged. By July nothing had changed: the bags still fluttered from every stall, still blocked every drain, still burned in every heap of refuse.

The failure was not one of intention but of preparation. No alternative had been made available at a price traders could afford; a paper bag cost five times as much as the plastic one it was meant to replace. The agency charged with enforcement had forty inspectors for a state of eight million people. And the two factories that produced the bags, employing three thousand workers between them, had not been consulted at all — a silence they answered with a court injunction.

None of this was unforeseeable. Countries that have curbed plastic waste successfully did so gradually, beginning with a small levy, funding cheap alternatives, and bringing manufacturers into the process early enough to retool rather than resist. A ban is a headline; a transition is a plan. The state had produced the first and mistaken it for the second.

passages.title: The apprentice
passages.text:
Emeka was fourteen when his father handed him to Oga Cletus, a spare-parts dealer at Ladipo, with the words that every Igbo apprentice hears: 'He is your son now. Whatever he does, do to him.' For six years Emeka would not be paid. He would sweep the shop, carry goods, learn the names and prices of ten thousand parts, and, if he served faithfully, be 'settled' at the end with capital to open his own stall.

Foreign economists who have studied the system call it the largest business incubator in the world, and they are not exaggerating. It transfers skills, credit and customers from one generation of traders to the next without banks, business schools or government agencies. Its weakness is the same as its strength: everything depends on the character of the master. A fair one produces a fair trader; a cruel one produces a young man who has learnt only that power is to be abused.

Emeka was fortunate. At twenty he received a shop, a supplier's introduction and two hundred thousand naira. His first act as a trader was to travel home and ask his cousin's son whether he would like to learn a business.

questions.q: The 'older networks' referred to in the passage are
questions.B: the old telephone cables in the village
questions.C: the postal services of the colonial era
questions.D: the local radio stations she listened to
questions.explanation: The passage names these as the channels through which her news travelled.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Grandmother wept partly because
questions.A: she had missed the burial by two days
questions.B: her uncle had bought her a cheap phone
questions.D: she had quarrelled with her sister
questions.explanation: The letter arrived 'two days after the burial', and she grieved the six days she spent unaware.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The final sentence suggests that grandmother answered the phone quickly at night because she
questions.explanation: 'The voice of a woman who had once been late for a death' links her promptness to the funeral she missed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Which statement about grandmother is TRUE according to the passage?
questions.A: She never sent a text message.
questions.B: She learnt to text within a month.
questions.D: She kept the phone switched off at night.
questions.explanation: The passage says she never sent a text; she kept the phone charged and on under her pillow.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The phrase 'with considerable fanfare' suggests that the announcement was made
questions.D: with a great deal of publicity
questions.explanation: Fanfare means showy publicity.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Which of the following was NOT given as a reason for the ban's failure?
questions.D: market women protested in the streets
questions.explanation: Market women merely 'shrugged'; the three reasons listed are price, enforcement and the factories' injunction.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The factories responded to the ban by
questions.explanation: The 'silence they answered with a court injunction'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: 'A ban is a headline; a transition is a plan' means that
questions.A: newspapers oppose bans but support transitions
questions.B: bans work better than transitions in developing countries
questions.C: plans should be published as headlines in the newspapers
questions.D: announcing a ban is easy; managing change needs careful planning
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts publicity with the detailed preparation that successful countries carried out.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The writer's tone in the passage is
questions.explanation: The writer criticises the failure but explains how it could have been done properly.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The words 'He is your son now' indicate that the master
questions.A: adopts the boy legally as his own child
questions.B: will send the boy to school at his own expense
questions.C: must pay the boy a salary like a son
questions.D: takes full responsibility for the boy, including discipline
questions.explanation: 'Whatever he does, do to him' hands the father's authority to the master.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the passage, to be 'settled' means to be
questions.A: given capital to start one's own business
questions.B: given a house in the city
questions.C: paid a monthly salary at last
questions.D: sent back to one's village with gifts
questions.explanation: The passage explains that a faithful apprentice is settled 'with capital to open his own stall'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Economists call the system 'the largest business incubator in the world' because it
questions.A: is run by the government at very low cost
questions.B: trains more engineers than the universities
questions.C: operates in Ladipo, the largest market in Africa
questions.D: creates new traders by passing on skills, credit and customers
questions.explanation: The passage lists exactly these transfers, made 'without banks, business schools or government agencies'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: According to the passage, the system's greatest weakness is that
questions.A: it depends entirely on the character of the master
questions.B: it lasts too long for most young men
questions.C: it pays no salary for six years
questions.D: it excludes girls from the trade
questions.explanation: 'Everything depends on the character of the master.'

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Emeka's first act as a trader shows that he
questions.A: wanted revenge on Oga Cletus for the six years
questions.B: wished to leave Ladipo and return home
questions.C: did not trust strangers with his new shop
questions.D: intended to continue the tradition that had helped him
questions.explanation: He went home to offer his cousin's son the same opportunity.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Kunle's excuses cut no ice with the principal.
questions.A: The principal was not persuaded by Kunle's excuses
questions.B: The principal punished Kunle for giving excuses
questions.C: Kunle gave the principal a cold reception
questions.explanation: 'To cut no ice with someone' means to have no influence on them.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The new manager is a chip off the old block.
questions.A: The manager closely resembles his father in character
questions.C: The manager was promoted from the workshop
questions.D: The manager is stubborn and unreasonable
questions.explanation: A 'chip off the old block' is a person very like one parent.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Ada would not hear of her daughter dropping out of school.
questions.A: Ada was deaf to her daughter's request
questions.B: Ada did not know her daughter had dropped out
questions.C: Ada refused to allow her daughter to drop out
questions.D: Ada's daughter did not tell her she had dropped out
questions.explanation: 'Would not hear of' = would not allow or consider.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The senator's promise turned out to be a pie in the sky.
questions.A: The senator kept his promise generously
questions.C: The senator promised to feed the people
questions.D: The promise was pleasant but impossible to achieve
questions.explanation: 'Pie in the sky' is a pleasant idea that will never happen.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Bimpe has a bone to pick with her landlord.
questions.A: Bimpe has a complaint to raise with her landlord
questions.B: Bimpe wants to eat with her landlord
questions.D: Bimpe and her landlord are good friends
questions.explanation: 'A bone to pick with someone' is a grievance to discuss.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The coach told the players to pull their socks up.
questions.A: The players were told to dress properly
questions.B: The players were told to stop playing
questions.C: The players were told to improve their performance
questions.D: The players were told to warm up
questions.explanation: 'Pull your socks up' means make an effort to improve.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: For all his wealth, Chief Okonkwo is a very lonely man.
questions.A: Chief Okonkwo is lonely because he is wealthy
questions.B: Chief Okonkwo's wealth has made him unpopular
questions.C: Chief Okonkwo spends all his wealth on friends
questions.D: Although he is wealthy, Chief Okonkwo is lonely
questions.explanation: 'For all' here means 'in spite of'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Hardly had the rain stopped when the traders returned to their stalls.
questions.A: The traders returned immediately after the rain stopped
questions.B: The traders returned before the rain stopped
questions.C: The traders barely returned because of the rain
questions.D: The rain hardly stopped, so the traders did not return
questions.explanation: 'Hardly ... when' expresses one event following another immediately.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The minister was economical with the truth.
questions.B: The minister spoke briefly and honestly
questions.C: The minister deliberately left out important facts
questions.D: The minister told the whole truth
questions.explanation: A polite way of saying someone was misleading by omission.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Ngozi's application fell through at the last minute.
questions.D: Ngozi's application failed at the final stage
questions.explanation: 'Fall through' means fail to be completed.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Uche could not make head or tail of the instructions.
questions.A: Uche could not understand the instructions at all
questions.B: Uche did not know where the instructions began
questions.C: Uche lost the first and last pages
questions.D: Uche refused to read the instructions
questions.explanation: 'Cannot make head or tail of' = cannot understand.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The candidate's speech was met with stony silence.
questions.B: The audience threw stones at the candidate
questions.C: The audience showed cold disapproval by saying nothing
questions.D: The audience was too tired to react
questions.explanation: 'Stony silence' is a hostile, unresponsive silence.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: Musa passed the examination by the skin of his teeth.
questions.explanation: 'By the skin of one's teeth' = only just.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: No sooner had the lights gone out than the generator came on.
questions.A: The generator came on immediately after the lights went out
questions.B: The generator came on before the lights went out
questions.C: The generator failed when the lights went out
questions.D: The lights went out because of the generator
questions.explanation: 'No sooner ... than' = immediately after.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence: The two brothers do not see eye to eye on the inheritance.
questions.A: The brothers cannot look at each other
questions.B: The brothers have not seen the inheritance
questions.C: The brothers disagree about the inheritance
questions.D: The brothers share the inheritance equally
questions.explanation: 'See eye to eye' = agree.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The council's decision to demolish the market was widely CONDEMNED.
questions.explanation: To condemn is to express strong disapproval.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The old man gave a LUCID account of the accident.
questions.explanation: Lucid means clearly expressed and easy to understand.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The witness was RELUCTANT to name the attackers.
questions.explanation: Reluctant means hesitant or unwilling.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The drug has a DETRIMENTAL effect on the liver.
questions.explanation: Detrimental means causing harm.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: His answers were so AMBIGUOUS that nobody knew what he meant.
questions.explanation: Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The committee will SCRUTINISE every receipt.
questions.explanation: To scrutinise is to inspect in detail.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The principal's decision was FINAL and could not be appealed.
questions.explanation: Final here means conclusive, allowing no further argument.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The team showed remarkable RESILIENCE after losing the first match.
questions.explanation: Resilience is the capacity to recover quickly from difficulties.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The hall was filled to CAPACITY.
questions.explanation: Capacity is the maximum amount a space can hold.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The governor's remarks INCENSED the youths.
questions.explanation: To incense is to make very angry.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: Her argument was so COGENT that the panel changed its mind.
questions.explanation: Cogent means clear, logical and convincing.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The doctor prescribed a PROLONGED course of treatment.
questions.explanation: Prolonged means continuing for a long time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The company was accused of FLOUTING the safety regulations.
questions.explanation: To flout is to openly disobey.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The village was left DESOLATE after the flood.
questions.explanation: Desolate means empty, bleak and abandoned.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capitals: The principal spoke to the parents in a CONCILIATORY tone.
questions.explanation: Conciliatory means intended to reduce anger and restore goodwill.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The mechanic gave a very PESSIMISTIC assessment of the car.
questions.explanation: Pessimistic (expecting the worst) is opposed by optimistic/hopeful.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The new road has made the village more ACCESSIBLE.
questions.explanation: Accessible (easy to reach) is the opposite of cut off / inaccessible.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The judge was known for his LENIENT sentences.
questions.explanation: Lenient (merciful) is the opposite of severe/harsh.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The two partners were in complete HARMONY over the plan.
questions.explanation: Harmony is the opposite of discord (disagreement).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The committee's report was remarkably CONCISE.
questions.explanation: Concise (short and to the point) is opposed by long-winded/verbose.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The senator gave a VAGUE answer to the question.
questions.explanation: Vague is the opposite of precise/specific.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The shop sells only GENUINE spare parts.
questions.explanation: Genuine is the opposite of fake/counterfeit.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The soldiers showed great COURAGE under fire.
questions.explanation: Courage is the opposite of cowardice.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The workers were praised for their DILIGENCE.
questions.explanation: Diligence (careful hard work) is opposed by laziness/negligence.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The price of tomatoes has been very STABLE this year.
questions.explanation: Stable is the opposite of fluctuating/unsteady.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The chairman gave a TERSE reply to the reporter.
questions.explanation: Terse (brief and abrupt) is opposed by lengthy/wordy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The witness's account was entirely CREDIBLE.
questions.explanation: Credible is the opposite of incredible/unbelievable.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The land was FERTILE and produced two harvests a year.
questions.explanation: Fertile is the opposite of barren/infertile.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: It is COMPULSORY for all students to attend the assembly.
questions.explanation: Compulsory is the opposite of optional/voluntary.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capitals: The minister's speech was full of OPTIMISM about the economy.
questions.explanation: Optimism is the opposite of pessimism/despair.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Neither the principal nor the teachers ____ aware of the change in the timetable.
questions.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('teachers' — plural).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The committee ____ divided in its opinion on the matter.
questions.explanation: Here the committee acts as one body ('its opinion'), so a singular verb is used.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: If I ____ the minister, I would resign immediately.
questions.explanation: The subjunctive 'were' is used for an unreal present condition.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Each of the boys ____ given a prize.
questions.explanation: 'Each' is singular and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The news ____ so shocking that she fainted.
questions.explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She insisted that he ____ the money before Friday.
questions.explanation: After 'insisted that', the bare subjunctive 'return' is used.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: By the time the police arrived, the thieves ____.
questions.explanation: The past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The man ____ car was stolen has reported to the police.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession (the man's car).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Ngozi is ____ than any other girl in the class.
questions.explanation: Comparative 'taller' is used with 'than'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I would rather you ____ the truth now.
questions.explanation: 'Would rather + subject' takes the past tense for a present wish.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The students, as well as their teacher, ____ present at the ceremony.
questions.explanation: 'As well as' does not change the number of the subject; 'students' is plural.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: There ____ a lot of furniture in the room.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Scarcely had he sat down ____ the phone rang.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely ... when' (not 'than', which follows 'no sooner').

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The teacher, together with the students, ____ to the museum.
questions.explanation: 'Together with' does not make the subject plural; 'teacher' is singular.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: This is the house ____ my father was born.
questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces a relative clause of place.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Adamu is one of the students who ____ selected for the competition.
questions.explanation: The relative clause refers to 'the students' (plural): 'who were selected'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Everybody ____ to bring ____ own writing materials.
questions.explanation: 'Everybody' is singular: 'is ... his or her'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The government has ____ a new policy on education.
questions.explanation: To 'bring out' a policy is to publish or introduce it; 'bring up' is to raise a child or topic.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The driver was charged ____ dangerous driving.
questions.explanation: One is 'charged with' an offence.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: She is very good ____ mathematics but poor ____ English.
questions.explanation: 'Good at' and 'poor at' a subject.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The doctor advised him to abstain ____ alcohol.
questions.explanation: 'Abstain from' is the correct preposition.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: I look forward to ____ from you soon.
questions.explanation: 'Look forward to' is followed by a noun or gerund.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: ____ the heavy rain, the match went ahead.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' takes a noun phrase; 'in spite' needs 'of'; 'although' needs a clause.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The twins are so alike that I cannot tell one from ____.
questions.explanation: With two, 'one ... the other'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The old man has lived in this village ____ over forty years.
questions.explanation: 'For' introduces a length of time; 'since' would need a starting point such as a year.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: MY father bought the car last year.
questions.A: Did your father buy the car last year?
questions.B: Did your mother buy the car last year?
questions.C: Did his father buy the car last year?
questions.D: Did your father sell the car last year?
questions.explanation: Stress on MY contrasts whose father it was.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The students WALKED to the stadium.
questions.A: Did the students drive to the stadium?
questions.B: Did the teachers walk to the stadium?
questions.C: Did the students walk to the school?
questions.D: Did the students walk to the stadium yesterday?
questions.explanation: Stress on WALKED contrasts the manner of going.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Amaka bought THREE textbooks yesterday.
questions.A: Did Amaka buy three textbooks today?
questions.B: Did Amaka buy two textbooks yesterday?
questions.C: Did Amaka buy three notebooks yesterday?
questions.D: Did Ngozi buy three textbooks yesterday?
questions.explanation: Stress on THREE contrasts the number.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The doctor examined the patient in the MORNING.
questions.A: Did the nurse examine the patient in the morning?
questions.B: Did the doctor examine the patient in the evening?
questions.C: Did the doctor examine the visitor in the morning?
questions.D: Did the doctor discharge the patient in the morning?
questions.explanation: Stress on MORNING contrasts the time.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: Tunde gave his SISTER the money.
questions.A: Did Tunde give his brother the money?
questions.B: Did Tunde lend his sister the money?
questions.C: Did Segun give his sister the money?
questions.D: Did Tunde give his sister the book?
questions.explanation: Stress on SISTER contrasts the receiver.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The farmers planted MAIZE on the new land.
questions.A: Did the farmers plant maize on the old land?
questions.B: Did the farmers plant cassava on the new land?
questions.C: Did the traders plant maize on the new land?
questions.D: Did the farmers harvest maize on the new land?
questions.explanation: Stress on MAIZE contrasts the crop.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: We watched the match at HOME.
questions.A: Did you watch the match at the stadium?
questions.B: Did you watch the film at home?
questions.C: Did they watch the match at home?
questions.D: Did you play the match at home?
questions.explanation: Stress on HOME contrasts the place.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the option to which the given sentence relates when the word in capitals is stressed: The principal PRAISED the students for their behaviour.
questions.A: Did the teacher praise the students for their behaviour?
questions.B: Did the principal scold the students for their behaviour?
questions.C: Did the principal praise the teachers for their behaviour?
questions.D: Did the principal praise the students for their results?
questions.explanation: Stress on PRAISED contrasts the action.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: PEAR
questions.explanation: 'Pear' is /peə/, rhyming with 'hair'; the others have /ɪə/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: WEIGHT
questions.explanation: 'Weight' is /weɪt/, rhyming with 'gate'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: TOMB
questions.explanation: 'Tomb' is /tuːm/, rhyming with 'room'; the 'b' is silent.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: DOUGH
questions.explanation: 'Dough' is /dəʊ/, rhyming with 'though'; the others end in /f/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: QUAY
questions.explanation: 'Quay' is pronounced /kiː/, rhyming with 'key'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that rhymes with the word in capitals: DEBT
questions.explanation: 'Debt' is /det/ (silent 'b'), rhyming with 'bet'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): geography
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-graphy' are stressed on the syllable before it: ge-O-gra-phy.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): electricity
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-ity' are stressed on the syllable before it: e-lec-TRI-ci-ty.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): photograph
questions.explanation: PHO-to-graph — stress on the first syllable (compare pho-TO-gra-phy).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): understand
questions.explanation: un-der-STAND — final-syllable stress.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): vegetable
questions.explanation: VE-ge-ta-ble is stressed on the first syllable (three syllables in speech: VEG-ta-ble).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): communication
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-tion' are stressed on the syllable before it: com-mu-ni-CA-tion.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): politician
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-cian' are stressed on the syllable before it: po-li-TI-cian.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): advertisement
questions.explanation: British English: ad-VER-tise-ment.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'record' as a VERB is stressed
questions.explanation: Noun RE-cord, verb re-CORD — a common noun/verb stress shift.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: The word 'present' as a NOUN is stressed
questions.explanation: Noun PRE-sent (a gift); verb pre-SENT.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): interesting
questions.explanation: IN-te-res-ting — first-syllable stress.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: In the following word, choose the option that has the correct stress pattern (the stressed syllable is written in capitals): thermometer
questions.explanation: Words ending in '-meter' (instruments) are stressed on the syllable before: ther-MO-me-ter.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: pOOl
questions.explanation: 'Pool' has the long /uː/, as in 'food'; the others have short /ʊ/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: bIRd
questions.explanation: 'Bird' has /ɜː/, as in 'word'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: cOAt
questions.explanation: 'Coat' has /əʊ/, as in 'note'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: shIP
questions.explanation: 'Ship' has short /ɪ/, as in 'sit'; the others have long /iː/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: cAUght
questions.explanation: 'Caught' has /ɔː/, as in 'court'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: baTH
questions.explanation: 'Bath' ends in voiceless /θ/, as in 'cloth'; the others have voiced /ð/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: CHemist
questions.explanation: 'Chemist' begins with /k/, as in 'school'; the others have /tʃ/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: naTIon
questions.explanation: 'Nation' has /ʃ/ in '-tion', as in 'station'; 'nature' and 'question' have /tʃ/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: laUGH
questions.explanation: 'Laugh' ends in /f/, as in 'cough'; the others have a silent 'gh'.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letters in capitals: Cell
questions.explanation: 'Cell' begins with /s/, as in 'city'; the others have /k/.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letter 'p' is SILENT.
questions.explanation: In 'pneumonia' the 'p' is not pronounced (/njuːˈməʊniə/).

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.q: Choose the word in which the letter 'h' is SILENT.
questions.explanation: 'Honest' is pronounced /ˈɒnɪst/ — the 'h' is silent.
